lessons.title: Air and its composition
lessons.programRef: Form 1 Basic Science — Air, water, energy, hygiene and environment (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe tests for oxygen and carbon dioxide.
reviewNotes: Composition values are standard approximations; carbon dioxide level is about 0.04 % (it changes slowly).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: What is in air?
blocks.md: Air is a **mixture** of gases: about **78 % nitrogen**, **21 % oxygen**, about **1 % argon and other gases**, and a very small amount (about 0.04 %) of **carbon dioxide**. It also contains **water vapour**, which varies from place to place. Air has mass, takes up space and exerts pressure.

blocks.caption: Approximate percentage by volume of the main gases in dry air.
blocks.alt: A bar chart: nitrogen 78, oxygen 21 and other gases 1 (percent).

blocks.title: Tests and uses
blocks.md:
- **Oxygen** relights a glowing splint; it is used in respiration and burning.
- **Carbon dioxide** turns **limewater milky**; plants use it for photosynthesis.
- **Nitrogen** is unreactive; plants need it in the soil as nitrates.
- **Burning** (combustion) needs oxygen: a candle in a closed jar goes out when most of the oxygen has been used, and the water level in the jar rises by about one fifth.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Air is not pure oxygen: most of it is nitrogen.
- Carbon dioxide is a gas that puts out flames; oxygen helps things burn.
- A closed container of air does not contain 'nothing': it contains gas with mass.

blocks.title: Oxygen used by a candle
blocks.statement: In an experiment, 100 cm³ of air is left over iron wool until 79 cm³ of gas remains. Estimate the percentage of oxygen in the air.

blocks.title: Identify the gas
blocks.statement: A gas relights a glowing splint. Another turns limewater milky. Name each gas.
steps: Relighting a glowing splint is the test for oxygen.
Turning limewater milky is the test for carbon dioxide.

lessons.title: Water and the water cycle
lessons.programRef: Form 1 Basic Science — Air, water, energy, hygiene and environment (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: State the uses of water and the steps in making water safe to drink.
reviewNotes: Water treatment steps are simplified; health advice (boiling time, chlorine) to be confirmed with a health worker or water authority.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: The water cycle
blocks.md: The Sun's heat makes water **evaporate** from seas, rivers and lakes (and plants lose water vapour). The vapour rises, cools and **condenses** to form clouds. Water falls as **rain** (precipitation), collects in rivers and underground, and flows back to the sea. The cycle is driven by the Sun.

blocks.caption: The water cycle.
blocks.alt: A picture with the sun, a cloud, the sea and land. Arrows show evaporation upward, condensation to a cloud, rain falling and run-off back to the sea.

blocks.title: Making water safe
blocks.md: Water for drinking must be free of germs and harmful chemicals. In a town it is **screened**, left to settle, **filtered** through sand and gravel, and treated with **chlorine** to kill germs. At home, water of doubtful quality can be **boiled** for several minutes, kept in a clean covered container and used with clean cups. Dirty water can spread diseases such as cholera and typhoid.

blocks.title: Tests for water
blocks.md:
- **Anhydrous copper(II) sulphate** (white) turns **blue** with water.
- **Cobalt chloride paper** turns from **blue to pink**.
- Pure water **boils at 100 °C** and **freezes at 0 °C** at sea level; a solution of salt boils above 100 °C.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Clear water is not always safe: germs cannot be seen.
- Filtering through sand does not kill germs; boiling or chlorine does.
- Rain falls from clouds that formed by condensation, not by boiling.

blocks.title: How long will a tank last?
blocks.statement: A tank holds 1000 L. Five people use about 25 L each per day. How many days will it last?

blocks.title: Test a liquid
blocks.statement: White copper sulphate powder turns blue when a few drops of a liquid are added. What does this show?
steps: The change from white to blue is the test for water.
It shows that the liquid contains water, not that it is pure.

lessons.title: Forms and sources of energy
lessons.programRef: Form 1 Basic Science — Air, water, energy, hygiene and environment (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Name the forms of energy and give examples.
Describe energy changes and state that energy is conserved.
reviewNotes: Check electricity sources: names of stations (Edéa, Song Loulou on the Sanaga; Lagdo on the Benue) are well known but should be confirmed; proportions of the mix not stated.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: What is energy?
blocks.md: **Energy** is the ability to do work or make something happen. It is measured in **joules (J)**. Forms of energy include **kinetic** (moving things), **potential** (stored by height or stretch), **heat**, **light**, **sound**, **electrical**, **chemical** (food, fuel, batteries) and **nuclear**.

blocks.caption: Energy changes in a hydroelectric power station.
blocks.alt: Four boxes joined by arrows: water in a dam, moving water, turbine and generator, electricity to homes.

blocks.title: Energy changes and conservation
blocks.md: Energy is **changed** from one form to another but is never created or destroyed: this is the **conservation of energy**. Some energy always becomes unwanted heat. Examples: a torch changes chemical energy to electrical, then to light and heat; a muscle changes chemical energy from food to kinetic energy and heat.

blocks.title: Sources of energy
blocks.md: **Renewable** sources do not run out: sunlight, wind, flowing water (hydroelectricity), biomass. **Non-renewable** sources will run out: coal, oil, natural gas. In Cameroon much electricity comes from dams on rivers such as the Sanaga (Edéa and Song Loulou), as well as gas and oil power stations.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Energy is not 'used up': it changes into other forms such as heat.
- A stretched elastic band stores potential energy; it is not moving.
- Firewood is a renewable source only if trees are replanted.

blocks.title: Energy chain
blocks.statement: Write the energy changes when a cook burns charcoal to warm water for a bath.
steps: Burning changes it into heat (and light), which warms the water.

blocks.title: Classify the sources
blocks.statement: Sort into renewable and non-renewable: sunlight, petrol, wind, coal.
steps: Sunlight and wind are replaced naturally.
Petrol and coal take millions of years to form.
blocks.answer: Renewable: sunlight, wind. Non-renewable: petrol, coal.

lessons.title: Hygiene, waste and the environment
lessons.programRef: Form 1 Basic Science — Air, water, energy, hygiene and environment (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: State good habits of personal and community hygiene.
Classify waste and describe how to manage it.
Name types of pollution and their effects.
reviewNotes: Health and hygiene advice is conservative but must be reviewed by a health worker; check the local names of waste-collection practice.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Personal and community hygiene
blocks.md: **Hygiene** means keeping clean to stay healthy. Wash your hands with soap and clean water **before eating or preparing food and after using the toilet**. Keep nails short, brush your teeth, bathe regularly, wash fruit and vegetables, cover food, use latrines and keep drains and compounds clean. Do not leave water standing where mosquitoes can breed.

blocks.caption: Managing waste: reduce, reuse, recycle, compost.
blocks.alt: Four boxes: reduce means use less; reuse means use again; recycle means make new items; compost turns food waste into soil.

blocks.title: Waste and pollution
blocks.md: **Biodegradable** waste rots naturally (peelings, leaves). **Non-biodegradable** waste does not (plastic bags, bottles, metal). **Pollution** is the addition of harmful substances to the environment: **air** (smoke, fumes), **water** (sewage, oil, chemicals) and **soil** (rubbish, chemicals). Plastic bags can block drains and cause floods.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Burning rubbish is not a safe way to get rid of it: the smoke is harmful.
- Throwing waste in a river pollutes the water that others drink.
- Recycling is not the same as reuse: reuse needs no change of the item.

blocks.title: Sort the waste
blocks.statement: Sort into biodegradable and non-biodegradable: banana peel, plastic bottle, dry leaves, tin can.
steps: Peel and leaves rot and are food for decomposers.
A plastic bottle and a tin can do not rot quickly.
blocks.answer: Biodegradable: banana peel, dry leaves. Non-biodegradable: plastic bottle, tin can.

blocks.title: Choose an action
blocks.statement: A family wants to reduce the plastic bags it throws away. Suggest two actions.
steps: Reduce: carry a basket to the market instead of taking new bags.
Reuse: use strong bags many times.
blocks.answer: Carry a reusable basket and reuse bags.
